C is joined to A, B, D, and E in one direction or the other, so the only nodes returned are F and G, shown in the accent color. The card lists F, G." width="100%"} Returns every node in the graph except the specified node itself and its direct neighbors. It is the complement of the node's closed neighborhood: all node IDs minus `neighbors(node, mode="all")` minus `node` itself. This is useful for: - building a candidate pool for link prediction or "people you may know" style recommendations (any new edge must go to a non-neighbor) - finding which parts of the graph a node is not directly connected to - sampling negative (non-edge) pairs for training or evaluation In a directed graph, a node counts as a neighbor if there is an edge in *either* direction, so both predecessors and successors are excluded. Non-neighbors may still be reachable through longer paths; this method only looks at direct adjacency. The cost is linear in the number of nodes and edges, and on large, sparse graphs the result is nearly the whole node set. The selection is not changed. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The reference node, given as an integer node ID or a string label. An unknown ID or label raises `ValueError`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Sorted list of node IDs that are not neighbors of `node=` (in either direction) and are not `node=` itself. Empty if the node is adjacent to every other node. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this 5-node directed path, node `2` connects only to `1` (incoming) and `3` (outgoing), so everything else -- `4` and `5` -- comes back as a non-neighbor: ::: {#bcf7c30c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=True) graph.add_path_graph(5) # 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 graph.get_non_neighbors(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [4, 5] ``` ::: ::: This makes a useful candidate pool for recommending new connections -- for example, ranking candidates by how many neighbors they already share with the target node. "C" shares neighbor "B" with "A", while "D" is isolated and shares none: ::: {#d1497ef2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) candidates = graph.get_non_neighbors("A") [ (graph.get_label_from_id(c), len(graph.get_common_neighbors("A", c))) for c in candidates ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('C', 1), ('D', 0)] ``` ::: :::
